item.title: Hormuz talks positive, Oman says, as Iran warns deal would not open strait
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c934j5y2lq9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Hormuz talks positive, Oman says, as Iran warns deal would not open strait - Published Oman has said positive talks have been taking place with Iran over an agreement to secure a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, as Tehran warned that any deal would not see an immediate reopening of the vital waterway. Both sides suggested on Saturday that discussions were progressing, but a timeline on any deal being finalised remained unclear. Oman's foreign ministry warned against attacks on shipping that could hamper that. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said talks were in their final stages but the reopening of the strait remained "subject to other conditions". Tehran has effectively blockaded the waterway, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and natural gas usually flows, since the US and Israel began attacking it in February. Talks in recent days have focused on the possibility of a deal between Iran and Oman on a new route through the strait, which they would both have responsibility for and is hoped would lead to progress in resuming shipping traffic. But Araghchi said a full reopening of the typically busy maritime route depended on other conditions being met, of which he provided a cursory appraisal. He said the conditions included Iran receiving compensation from the US for what Tehran described as violations of the deal both sides signed in June to cease fighting and advance talks to end the war. That deal - called a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) - quickly fell through, as did diplomatic talks, with tit-for-tat attacks resuming just days after it was signed. Separately, Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, Iran's security chief, told the semi-official news agency Tasnim that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until the US "corrects" its behaviour. He said the US needed to meet six Iranian demands, including a halt to threats against Iran, removal of its naval blockade of Iranian ports and release of Iran's frozen assets. Another blockade, on Saudi Arabia's ports in the Red Sea, had been imposed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis since 20 July. Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump said a deal with Iran "could be soon", but Vice-President JD Vance appeared to be more sceptical on Saturday, telling Fox News that work remained to be done even if progress was being made. "We're really in the middle of the game here," he said. "This thing is not over." Vance added that "we're applying a whole host of tools - diplomatic, economic [and] military tools - to ensure that we get the best outcome for the American people". Additionally, he claimed that the "same amount of oil" will emerge from the Gulf as did before the US military operation began on 28 February, although he offered no details. "What we're really working through now is how you can actually set up a traffic scheme so that the ships can pass through safely," he added. One of the main points of disagreement between Tehran and Washington has been Iran's reported threat to impose a fee on vessels wishing to cross the strait. Reuters - citing an Iranian official - previously reported that Tehran was seeking fees of between 5% and 7% of the price of cargoes from vessels who travel through it. Vance downplayed those reports, saying: "The Iranians have told us they have no plans to toll the Strait of Hormuz." Oman's warning against attacks on ships in the strait came as the United Arab Emirates (UAE) said on Saturday that Iran had targeted a tanker affiliated with Adnoc, its state-owned oil company, as it passed through. The UAE's foreign ministry said in a statement that a "hostile Iranian attack" had hit an Adnoc tanker "with a missile". It added that there were no casualties. Later on Saturday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency also reported a ship being struck by "an unknown projectile" off the coast of Oman, causing "a fire that has been extinguished" but no casualties. It is unclear whether UKMTO was referring to the same ship as the UAE. Related topics - Published3 days ago - Published4 days ago

item.title: Trump's ex-lawyer Todd Blanche narrowly confirmed as US attorney general
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cewr898jy8go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump's ex-lawyer Todd Blanche narrowly confirmed as US attorney general - Published US President Donald Trump's former personal lawyer Todd Blanche has been narrowly confirmed as attorney general - the nation's top law enforcement official. The vote brings to an end a lengthy standoff between Senate Republicans and the Trump administration over Blanche, who has served as acting attorney general since April. Blanche won confirmation in a 50-49 vote overnight, with two Republican senators, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, joining all Democrats to oppose his nomination. Senator Bill Cassidy cast the deciding vote, a decision closely watched in Washington given the years of acrimony between the Louisiana Republican and Trump. After the vote, Blanche said he was "deeply honoured by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me". Some Republican senators had raised concerns about Blache's handling of the release of Jeffrey Epstein-related documents and his role in establishing Trump's $1.8bn (£1.3bn) "anti-weaponisation" fund. The fund was planned to provide compensation to individuals who alleged government persecution but critics including Murkowski feared it would go to individuals who were prosecuted for participating in the 6 January attack on Congress in 2021. Blanche eventually pledged to walk back the fund after blowback from Republican senators during his confirmation hearings. It remains unclear whether the commitment is legally binding or whether Trump could later persuade Blanche, his former personal attorney, to revive a similar scheme under another name. The issues surrounding Blanche meant Senators Collins and Murkowski held off from backing Blanche, with the latter citing her lack of confidence in Blanche to "check the worst impulses of this administration". Murkowski announced on Friday she would oppose Blanche, citing concerns over the "politicisation" of the justice department. Collins also raised concerns about Blanche's role in settling Trump's $10bn lawsuit with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), but said he ultimately trusted Blanche to give the president candid legal advice. Before casting the deciding vote, Cassidy announced that he believed Blanche was the best option the president would put forward. "This is not a referendum on President Trump, it is a decision regarding Mr Blanche, in very specific circumstances," said Cassidy on Friday. "All considered, I will vote for Mr Blanche." Cassidy acknowledged Trump is the ultimate decider on the direction of the justice department, but that Senate confirmation would give Blanche "greater leverage to push for things that should be pushed for." During Trump's second impeachment in 2021, Cassidy voted to convict Trump over the 6 January 2021 Capitol riot. The vote did not pass, and when Trump returned to office, he successfully forced Cassidy into retirement by backing a primary challenger for his Louisiana Senate seat earlier this year. In a post on X, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer expressed concern that Blanche's appointment would be an "excuse on a silver platter to keep up his pervasive, breathtaking corruption". "Todd Blanche has no intention of stopping Trump's corruption. He advanced his career enabling it," he wrote. "Every senator who voted to confirm him has now branded themselves as an enabler, too." But most Republicans swiftly celebrated the victory. Iowa Republican Senator Chuck Grassley - chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee - wrote on X that Blanche had shown "extraordinary patience, compassion [and] tenacity" throughout the appointment process. "There's no doubt he's qualified," Grassley wrote. Blanche was already deputy attorney general when he took up the interim leadership role in April, after Pam Bondi was fired.

item.title: US offers $1bn to Colombia on new right-wing president's first day of office
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9wy3y0e5wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US offers $1bn to Colombia on new right-wing president's first day of office - Published The US has pledged $1bn (£740m) to Colombia hours after the country's new right-wing populist president was sworn in. Abelardo de la Espriella, an admirer of Donald Trump who echoed many of the US president's policies on the campaign trail, used his maiden speech to promise an "all-out war" on drug cartels. The US state department said the "security package" would help him achieve "our shared goals", which include fighting organised crime and illegal immigration. Trump repeatedly criticised de la Espriella's left-wing predecessor over his approach to both. The inauguration is the latest in a wider trend of Latin American nations shifting rightwards on a backdrop of economic hardship and concerns about gang violence. Trump has taken a greater interest in Latin America during his second term, courting politically aligned leaders and spurning those with whom he disagrees. Before the election, Trump said de la Espriella had the "total support and strength of the United States behind him", predicting a "much better relationship" with Colombia after he was elected in June. A lawyer and businessman by trade, de la Espriella has cast himself as maverick outsider, vowing to combat crime with an "iron fist". In a fiery first official speech - addressing troops at a nearby military base - de la Espriella pledged to crush armed insurgents, rebuild Colombia and defend democracy "by reason or by force". He said in "the age of the Tiger" - a reference to his self-styled nickname - the state would be forceful and decisive against crime, adding: "There will not be a single place in our territory where criminals can feel safe." Comparisons have been drawn between de la Espriella's plans and similar crackdowns by similar right-wing populists Nayib Bukele and Daniel Noboa in El Salvador and Ecuador, respectively. This is in stark contrast to his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, who pursued what he called a "total peace" strategy to the country's internal armed conflict between guerrilla groups, the state and cartels, which prioritised negotiation and incentivising farmers to stop planting coca. Critics say the method failed. Membership of armed groups has expanded in recent years, and a brutal conflict between rival rebel groups along the Colombia-Venezuela border displaced tens of thousands of people last year. Colombia - and Petro's policies - have been among targets Trump has repeatedly blamed for the flow of drugs and illegal migrants into the US. Petro, for his part, was highly critical of Trump's influence on the region, as well as his administration's seizure of Venezuela's socialist President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, to stand trial on drug charges in the US, clearing the way for US firms to tap Venezuela's oil reserves. Petro, who could not stand for another term, and Iván Cepeda, the left-wing candidate he backed, had insisted Colombia should not become another "vassal" of the US. In one of his first acts as president, de la Espriella said Colombia would join the "Shield of the Americas" security partnership founded by Trump. The US state department welcomed the move, saying de la Espriella's "pro-growth agenda" had created an opportunity to "increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries". It also brings Colombia into league with other right-wing governments that have sought closer ties to the Trump administration, such as Argentina, whose libertarian President Javier Milei de le Espriella has said he admired. Argentina was the recipient of a $20bn US Treasury bailout, while Trump has said he would feel "a lot differently" about supporting the country if Milei was replaced by a left-wing president. In contrast, Trump has repeatedly threatened to give Cuba's Communist government similar treatment to Maduro's in Venezuela. De la Espriella's ascension - along with that of Keiko Fujimori in Peru - means that Brazil's Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva now has fewer political allies in the region as the number of left-wing leaders dwindles. However, he will face Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro - a far-right populist friendly with the US president - in October. De la Espriella has also promised a strong military alliance with the US and Israel, in stark contrast to Petro, who cut ties with the Israeli government over its offensive in Gaza and was a vocal advocate for the Palestinian cause. Who is Abelardo de la Espriella? He calls himself "El Tigre" - the tiger. A media-savvy lawyer and millionaire businessman, he cast himself as an "outsider" who refused to govern with "the usual suspects" - a reference to Colombia's pre-Petro political elite. The hardliner chose to take the oath of office not in Colombia's capital, Bogotá, but in the western city of Cali - signalling his desire to cast himself as apart from the centralised politics of the past. Before entering politics, he had a successful career as a defence lawyer representing drug-trafficking paramilitaries - the kinds of criminals he now intends to lock up. De la Espriella announced his candidacy a month after another conservative candidate was shot and killed, and regularly appeared at rallies behind bulletproof glass wearing a bulletproof vest - if not a Colombian football jersey. He has been a US citizen since 2023 after living and working in Miami for many years. Among attendees of his inauguration was US Attorney General Todd Blanche and Fifa president Gianni Infantino, who was accompanied by the head of South America's football governing body Conmebol as questions linger over his leadership.

item.title: Messi's father Jorge dies aged 68 after illness
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c70gn3w5ek5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Messi's father Jorge dies aged 68 after illness - Published Lionel Messi's father Jorge has died at the age of 68 following a long illness. Jorge, who had also been the Argentina forward's agent since he was 14, passed away in a hospital in his hometown of Rosario, Argentina, in the early hours of Saturday morning. After speculation about his health during this summer's World Cup, the Messi family issued a statement saying he was dealing with a "health-related situation" but did not disclose the nature of his condition. Jorge helped his son become arguably the best player of all time and was in Qatar to see Lionel end his quest to lead Argentina to their third World Cup triumph in 2022. The Inter Miami forward, 39, also became an eight-time Ballon d'Or winner and won the Champions League four times with Barcelona, plus 10 La Liga titles in 17 seasons in their first team. Jorge supported his local team Newell's Old Boys and Lionel joined the club when he was seven years old. The family relocated to Spain in February 2001 after Lionel was signed by Barca aged just 13, and although Messi's mother and three siblings soon moved back to Rosario, his father stayed with him in Barcelona. "Jorge was the pillar and the person who supported with vision, rigor and affection the career of the greatest player of all time alongside his wife, Celia Cuccittini," Newell's Old Boys posted on X., external "His constant companionship and behind-the-scenes leadership were essential in backing every step of Lionel, from his beginnings at Malvinas [youth academy] to the pinnacle of world football glory. "Thank you for teaching him to love these colours." The club added that they "embrace with affection Celia, Lionel, Rodrigo, Matias and Maria Sol, and all their loved ones and close ones in this difficult moment". Barcelona thanked Jorge "for his commitment to our club, for entrusting us with the beginnings and the most glorious years of his son Leo's football career". The Argentine Football Association said it "deeply mourns with sadness and sorrow the passing of Jorge Messi, father of our captain and emblem, Lionel Messi". It added: "From here, we stand in solidarity with the entire family during this difficult time and send the most heartfelt, warm and affectionate embrace." The Messi family responded after an Argentine television presenter falsely reported Jorge had died during Argentina's opening game at this summer's World Cup. The presenter later resigned, while the family expressed their "deep discomfort with the lack of sensitivity, respect and discretion with which some people have treated what is strictly a private family matter". - Published8 June - Published8 June

item.title: Madonna pays tribute to 'genius, otherworldly' producer William Orbit
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cewr8wel4z8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Madonna pays tribute to 'genius, otherworldly' producer William Orbit - Published Madonna has paid tribute to her regular collaborator and acclaimed music producer William Orbit, who died last month at the age of 69. "You pressed a magic button inside of me and I fell into a galaxy of unrealised dreams," the pop superstar wrote on Instagram on Saturday. "Your music gave me a magic carpet to fly on and I visited many places." Orbit's family announced "with profound sadness" on Friday that the Grammy-winning producer died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given. The British producer, whose real name was William Wainwright, helped reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with Ray of Light, an album that blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop. - Madonna and Blur producer William Orbit dies aged 69 - Published1 day ago With its genre-bending sound, Ray of Light went on to win three Grammy Awards and is still considered by many to be the Queen of Pop's greatest record. "I had an epiphany when I met you and started working with you," Madonna wrote in her post, alongside a video of herself standing beside Orbit to accept a Grammy Award. It also includes clips of the music videos and work she and Orbit created together. Madonna said Orbit inspired her to sing and write in ways she never had before, without caring if her words "made sense or not". "In many ways you were my Ray of Light - as was my daughter Lola who was born around this time," the singer wrote. At the time she began working with Orbit, Madonna said she was beginning a new chapter, and Orbit stayed by her side with his "genius way of hearing music". "The studio was often church-like and I would sit in silence, waiting for your ideas to explode out of your keyboard or your guitar and then I would run with them," she wrote. "I miss those days." In addition to Ray of Light, Orbit also worked with Madonna on her 2000 album Music and produced several tracks for her 2012 album work MDNA. The London-born producer was also renowned and sought-after for his production work, collaborating with artists from across the music world including Blur, Pink, U2, All Saints, Robbie Williams and Britney Spears. "You were so otherworldly. So singular," Madonna wrote in her tribute. The pop star said even though she worked with other producers over the years, she never forgot Orbit and "the magical time we spent together". "I was so lucky to have known you and fallen down the rabbit hole with you."

item.title: Paris tells e-scooter riders to wear safety gear or face fines
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89nkln7w7ko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Paris tells e-scooter riders to wear safety gear or face fines - Published Electric scooter riders in Paris face being fined if they fail to comply with new safety rules, as police try to curb the number of accidents in the French capital. Some 79 people were killed in e-scooter accidents last year, a sharp rise from the 45 who died the year prior, police said on Saturday, citing figures from France's road safety watchdog. In a bid to address "the concerning rise in serious and fatal accidents" involving the motorised vehicles, it is now mandatory for riders to wear a helmet and high-vis vest on public roads. Those who don't face fines of €135 (£129) for failing to wear an approved helmet, and smaller fines of €35 (£30) for not wearing a vest or retro-reflectors. The regulations also cover other electric transportation devices, such as electric unicycles and hoverboards. Official figures show that around 1,100 people were injured in e-scooter accidents in Paris last year, a rise of 33% on the year before. This is despite Paris banning rental e-scooters in 2023 over safety concerns, while allowing privately owned ones to continue being ridden. E-scooters remain popular with the commuters in the city, where narrow roads can become congested. Private e-scooter ownership in France is the highest in Europe, according to the EU. Some 2.5 million people owned e-scooters there as of 2023, with hundreds of thousands more purchased since. Many of these are thought to be in the capital, though exact figures are not kept. Existing rules in Paris ban e-scooter riding for under-14s, prohibit carrying passengers and set a maximum speed limits of 25km/h (16mph). Helmets and high-visibility vests are already mandatory in several French regions, including Seine-et-Marne, Alpes-Maritimes and Vaucluse. Paris was one of the first cities to adopt e-scooters, but growing concern about dangerous driving and obstructing pavements led to for-hire e-scooters being outlawed. Their fate was decided in a city-wide referendum, which saw 90% voters back a rental ban even though only 8% of eligible voters turned out. Other European cities have moved to ban rental e-scooters in recent years, with Madrid outlawing them in 2024 and Brussels announcing it will follow suit in June. item.title: Spain imposes border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yv5l6yr5ko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Spain imposes border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies - Published Spain has imposed border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy as a row between the two EU countries intensifies. The measures - which started at midnight (22:00 GMT) and will last for a month - come a week after Italy introduced similar restrictions following an influx of about 78,000 migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Spanish officials said the documents of 5%-10% of passengers were being checked before they were allowed to disembark planes. Italy has also said its border controls are random. The crisis has pitted Spain's socialist leader Pedro Sanchez against Italy's conservative leader Giorgia Meloni - who has long called for stricter EU migration rules. Italy does not share a land border with Spain. Its government said last week that decision to temporarily suspend the border-free Schengen arrangement was to prevent any of the migrants who had entered Ceuta from travelling on to Italy. Madrid dismissed this position, saying it was based on "spurious arguments" that lacked any basis in fact because the migrants who entered Ceuta had no way of entering the Schengen area. On Friday, Spain demanded Italy reverse its checks by Sunday. Rome said they would stay until at least 15 August - when, it said, Spain "expects a new wave of migration" to hit Ceuta. Italy has said that Spanish and EU citizens are exempt from additional checks when arriving in Italy, with these extra steps only for non-EU residents. However, it is not clear how border officials were meant to distinguish between EU and non-EU travellers and El Pais has reported that several Italian airport terminals have seen long queues and waiting times in recent days, with passengers arriving from Spain directed to a specific line for checks. As for Spanish controls, the authorities insists the immigration checks are random. However, a passenger arriving in Madrid on Saturday told national broadcaster RTVE that all passengers on her flight had had to show their passports. "They told us we couldn't get off the plane without showing our documents," Elisa said. Another passenger said "we were stopped and asked for identification, which the police seemed to approve of". Spain says its checks will stay in place until 7 September "unless a change in the circumstances that led to its adoption warrants modifying that period". Temporary suspensions of the Schengen agreement are not unprecedented. Italy also maintains controls on its border with Slovenia. Italy's decision to suspend Schengen for a month was backed by Finland and Denmark, while the Czech Republic called for Spain's membership to be temporarily suspended. Most of the migrants who arrived in Ceuta last week were returned within days. One hundred are believed to have died during the crossing. Nearly 1,400 minors, some of them "very young boys and girls", still remain there. Spain has not announced an anticipated second wave of crossings from Morocco. But BBC Arabic has found dozens of Facebook posts calling for a second crossing in mid-August, including some that advertised swimming equipment for sale. Six of these groups had more than 100,000 followers. Meta says it has removed posts that violate its policy. The Spanish prime minister's office told El Pais they were monitoring the situation but did not expect a repeat of scenes from last week. It remains unclear exactly why tens of thousands of migrants attempted to cross into Ceuta, but the EU's Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner has suggested criminal networks spreading disinformation were to blame - an assertion the Spanish government has agreed with. The crossings came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be summarily returned to Morocco. Morocco, for its part, has laid blame for the crisis on the court, with an unnamed government source briefing local outlets that "the deterrent element of the system collapsed and the dam gave way, not under the weight of the criminals, but of a judge's decision". The number of people swimming to Ceuta at once has raised questions about why Morocco's border guards did not attempt to stop them. The two exclaves have long been a bone of diplomatic contention between Spain and Morocco, which does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over them. item.title: Child among three killed in Russian missile attacks near Kyiv
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz7dy8gq99eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Child among three killed in Russian missile attacks near Kyiv - Published At least three people, including a child, have been killed in overnight Russian attacks near the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, a local official said. Another three people were injured as ballistic missiles hit east of Kyiv, head of the regional military administration Timur The new attack comes just days after 21 people were killed as Russia intensifies its strikes, aware that Ukraine has been running out of Western-donated interceptor missiles used to defend its skies. On Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky issued a fresh call for more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles, saying what his country was receiving was not enough. Zelensky's plea comes days after US President Donald Trump appeared to go back on a promise to grant Ukraine a licence to manufacture the defensive systems. On Saturday, Ukraine's president still referred to an agreement with the US on a licence. Since coming to office, Trump has scaled back direct military aid for Ukraine. Instead, Ukraine's European allies have been buying expensive US supplies - such as Patriot missiles - which are then donated to Ukraine. "Ukraine does not have, nor will it ever have, the sort of funds that Russia has, which it is using to finance the war," Zelensky said on Saturday. "We have what we need, thanks to European aid and support from other countries. But additional funding specifically for Ukrainian production is what is needed." Earlier in the week, Zelensky said the supply of interceptors from allies had been "significantly reduced" this year. The Ukrainian leader was speaking during his first trip to Serbia. He met President Aleksandar Vučić to discuss economic ties, security issues and relations with the European Union. Zelensky is trying to build wider support for Ukraine, but Vučić, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, has refused to impose sanctions on Russia. Serbia is trying to join the EU and has provided aid to Ukraine and promised to help it rebuild after the war. At the joint news conference with Zelensky in the capital, Belgrade, Vučić focused on Ukraine's European accession and pledged to support it. Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Since then, Russia has seized parts of Ukraine in the east, but the front lines have remained unchanged for a long time. Trump's efforts to mediate an end to the conflict have faltered recently, leading to an escalation of attacks between the two warring sides. Ukraine has developed advanced drones able to hit deep into Russian territory in an effort to take the war to Russia. In the latest such attack, the Ukrainian military hit Russia's Ilsky and Syzran oil refineries during overnight attacks, causing fires at both, the Ukrainian general staff said on Saturday. Moscow-linked vessels in the Black Sea were also hit - according to Zelensky the intention is to limit oil revenues used by Russia to "finance" its war. The Russia-Ukraine war has threatened to spill over into neighbouring countries. There have been several instances of drones or missiles flying into their territories. On most occasions, Russia has been blamed, but denied any involvement. On Saturday, a drone entered Bulgarian airspace and exploded near an international gas pipeline, its prime minister said, after crossing from Romania. Rumen Radev said it had been carrying a "significant" amount of explosives but there had been no casualties or reports of damage. Bulgaria's defence ministry said it appeared to be a Maya decoy drone, which is known to be used by Ukraine. "At the moment, there is no reason to believe that the incident was intentional," the ministry said. Later, Heorhii Tykhyi, spokesman for Ukraine's foreign ministry, was quoted as saying that "we can say with certainty that the Ukrainian Armed Forces did not intentionally direct any assets toward Bulgaria", but stopped short of admitting the drone was Ukrainian. item.title: Typhoon Dolphin batters Japan's Okinawa before bearing down on China
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvglp2zlvrlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Typhoon Dolphin batters Japan's Okinawa before bearing down on China - Published Typhoon Dolphin has cut power to at least 44,000 buildings and injured at least five people after hitting Japan's Okinawa island on Saturday. Flights to and from Okinawa's main airport - Naha International Airport - were cancelled as it closed on Friday as the storm arrived. The storm had maximum wind speeds of 162km/h (101mph) on Saturday and has been categorised as a "very strong" typhoon by the Japan Meteorological Agency, which warned of high waves, storm surges and lightning strikes. Dolphin is expected to make landfall on China's eastern coast late on Sunday or early on Monday. Authorities there have shut ports and schools ahead of its arrival. The main areas in Japan affected by the typhoon are the islands of Okinawa and Amami in the far south-west of the country. Five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the Okinawan prefectural government. Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said. Japan's national broadcaster NHK reports numerous accounts of trees being toppled by strong winds throughout Nago city in Okinawa, while a car was found overturned and leaking oil in a parking lot. In China, Zhejiang's Ningbo Lishe International Airport said it would stop its operations from 23:30 local time on Saturday (15:30 GMT) and suspend all flights on Sunday. A coastal typhoon alert in Zhejiang has been raised to its highest level, and port and ferry services have been halted in the Chinese province. Typhoon season in the western Pacific typically occurs between May and October, when typhoons are considered more commonplace. This year is a strong El Niño year, which experts say means typhoons can grow to be more intense. In an average year of 25 cyclones reaching tropical storm strength in the region, around three usually make landfall in Japan, according to the country's meteorological agency. Some of these will be strong enough to be classified as typhoons – as was the case with Dolphin. A typhoon is the term used for storms that form in the north-west Pacific, whereas a hurricane is the term used for storms that form in the Atlantic or eastern Pacific.

item.title: Fast-moving Canada wildfire doubles in size forcing thousands to flee homes
item.description:

Fast-moving Canada wildfire doubles in size forcing thousands to flee homes - Published Thousands of people were forced to flee their homes as a fast-moving wildfire in a remote part of western Canada spread rapidly, doubling in size since it was first detected on Friday. The Bald Range fire now occupies more than 36 sq miles (95 sq km) across the Summerland and Okanagan-Similkameen districts of British Columbia, according to the BC Wildfire Service. Erick Thompson, an emergency official with the Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen, said this was one of the "quickest-moving, largest fires in such a short time" he had seen in the fire-prone region. The fire remained "out of control" as of Saturday morning. The district of Summerland, which has a population of around 12,000, was ordered to evacuate. The power went out across the area, officials said early Saturday. Hundreds of residents living in Summerland care facilities, including senior housing, were being relocated to safer areas, according to Interior Health, a publicly funded health authority in BC. "Throughout the night and into this morning, first responders, BC Wildfire Service crews, [Royal Canadian Mounted Police] officers, emergency management teams, and local communities worked tirelessly to keep people safe and fight the fire near Summerland," BC Premier David Eby said on social media. "They continue to do everything possible to protect people and communities." It was not yet clear how many structures had been destroyed in the blaze. The nearby districts of Okanagan, Peachland, and Okanagan-Similkameen also issued evacuation orders, as well as evacuation alerts in some areas. On Friday evening, Thompson had been giving updates on the rapidly-spreading fire from the Okanagan-Similkameen emergency operations centre. The next morning, in a video posted from his car, he said he had left the centre to evacuate his own family. "I had to leave the EOC to come and get my family to leave this area. We're heading south," he said. In Okanagan, there are a lot of horses that residents have been struggling to evacuate, Canadian broadcaster CBC reported. Those unable to relocate their animals left their gates open in the hope the animals would find their own way to safety, local residents told CBC. Some owners also painted markings on their animals to make them easier to identify later, according to the outlet. Hundreds of wildfires have raged across Canada this summer, with nearly 200 burning in Ontario in July, sending air quality in Toronto to one of the worst levels in the world for a few days. Smoke from those Canadian wildfires drifted down into parts of the US, including Minnesota and New York, leading US President Donald Trump to threaten new tariffs on the US's northern neighbour. item.description:

========================================
Thai PM vows to introduce stricter gun laws after eight killed in shooting - Published Thailand's prime minister has vowed to introduce new gun control laws following a shooting by a teenager on the outskirts of Bangkok that left eight people dead and 22 injured. Fourteen people remain in hospital, seven of whom are in a critical condition. The 14-year-old killed his grandparents at the home they shared before travelling to Debsirin School in Nonthaburi, where he had been a student. There, he killed five teachers before taking his own life. Later, Thai media reported that a student had also died from their injuries. Speaking after the attack, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said he planned to introduce laws that restrict the carrying of firearms in public. - I was standing in front of my teacher when she was shot, Thai pupil says - Published1 day ago The new legislation will only allow government officials on duty to carry guns. Police Col Thadsakorn Konthong said that the gun and bullets used in the attack belonged to the teen's grandfather, with an initial inspection finding signs that the firearm had been searched for inside the grandfather's bedroom. International and local media have reported that the gun was legally registered and had a permit. Thailand has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in South East Asia, with around 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, around four million of which are believed to be owned illegally. The country has strict gun laws, which punish the illegal possession of arms with up to 10 years in jail, but enforcement of these laws has been an issue. During his time as interior minister, Anutin introduced a number of gun control laws, including a short-term ban on new gun licenses and import restrictions. Speaking on Friday, the prime minister said the tragedy "shouldn't have happened". "I don't just feel sorry for the victims but I feel sorry that this happened. How can this happen in our country," Anutin added. The teenager is believed to have shot his 73-year-old grandfather and 74-year-old grandmother at their two-storey flat at around 05:00 local time on Friday (22:00 GMT on Thursday). Each was killed by a single shot to the head, a Thai police official said. After killing his grandparents, the teenager boarded a school bus carrying the firearm and dozens of bullets, Reuters news agency reported. He then attended his first class at 08:30 and his second at 09:20. Around half an hour into his second class of the day, he drew the gun and began shooting. The teenager is believed to have first shot teachers on the school's sixth floor, killing three of them. "He then walked down the stairs and encountered the school's deputy director and the director's secretary, who were going up the stairs to check on the situation," Police Major General Dejrapee Kongdee told Reuters. "The attacker shot and killed both of them on the staircase." Police were deployed to the scene while the shooting was ongoing. They found the attacker, who by then had shot himself, around 10:40, Dejrapee said. Five people were immediately killed and at least 23 were wounded. Later, Thailand's public broadcaster and the Bangkok Post reported that an eighth victim had died. National police chief Gen Kittiratt Phanphet told reporters that forensic officers had found the attacker's shots were quite accurate, with several hitting vital spots on the body. The prime minister said the attack was "well prepared" with "clear steps and clear goals". According to local media, police have searched devices belonging to the teenager and found several videos relating to school shootings in the US. The teenager has been described as quiet and well behaved by family members in local media. His uncle told Thai media the teen spent much of his time indoors playing violent video games and rarely went outside. He added there was no indication the teenager was planning the attack. The attacker had lived with his grandparents, as his parents were divorced. The Debsirin School, founded in Bangkok in 1885, is one of Thailand's top secondary schools with branches across the country. It counts many prominent Thai figures among its alumni, from diplomats and athletes to several prime ministers.

item.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign defence pact
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c30418m4mj4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign defence pact - Published Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have signed a joint defence agreement, saying an attack on one of them would be seen as an attack on all three. The pact was announced at a meeting between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in the Saudi city of Mecca. After the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February, Tehran and its allies struck targets in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states and disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a major oil shipping channel, and the Red Sea. The Mecca agreement has drawn a sharp reaction from Tehran, where an senior member of parliament said it would not help Saudi Arabia. "The Saudis should know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan does not bring them security, just as years of unilateral milking of the Americans did not bring them security," Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of National Security commission, wrote on his X. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had already announced a joint defence pact last year. The new Mecca Joint Defence Agreement sees three of the world's most powerful Muslim nations come together to offer mutual defence guarantees. It aims "to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three States shall be regarded as an attack against them all", a joint statement reads. "It further provides for the enhancement of all aspects of defence co-operation among the three States." Although the pact pledges mutual support, it provides no specifics on the obligations of each party. A Turkish official quoted by Reuters news agency said the pact was "purely defensive in nature". Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey each bring different qualities to the table, with each wanting something different out of it. For the Saudis, this gives an extra level of security in a region whose security architecture has been upended by the US and Israel's war with Iran. Last month, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels – who control much of the north-west of the country - announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and targeted Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. Furthermore, the Saudis will be keenly aware of last year's Israeli strikes on Doha, targeting senior Hamas officials. According to a report last year by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, external, "across the Gulf, states recalibrated their defence strategies". This pact is one of Saudi Arabia's responses. For Pakistan, the pact offers different but complementary benefits. In May 2025 its long-standing tensions with India boiled over into open conflict. While an all-out war was avoided, having the economic muscle of Saudi Arabia and the military and industrial might of Turkey in their corner will be seen as increasingly valuable. It also comes at a time when Pakistan has been taking on a far more significant role in global diplomacy. It has acted as an intermediary between Iran and the US and hosted ceasefire negotiations, significantly increasing its status in the region - something this pact further cements. As for Turkey, the benefits are different. According to Burcu Ozcelik from the London-based Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), the deal offers opportunities for the country's significant defence industries through "joint production, technology partnerships, procurement and greater military interoperability". While, on the surface, the concept of a mutual defence agreement seems straightforward, in practice the circumstances in which they would come into play are both complex and uncertain. Would, for example, Turkey be obliged to join in strikes on Yemen if Saudi Arabia's full-scale war with the Houthis were to restart? Would Saudi Arabia have to declare war on India were there to be a re-emergence of conflict with Pakistan? Each instance would require complex calculations and careful diplomacy, often in an attempt to avoid escalation. It is, in short, uncertain. The one consequence of a mutual defence agreement that sides involved will be banking on, however, is deterrence. The very fact that they each now have two other regional powers standing behind them may not make aggression impossible, but it will make its potential cost significantly higher. Spanish police arrest 78 people in bust of 'one of largest' smuggling networks - Published One of the largest criminal networks smuggling drugs and people in the western Mediterranean has been dismantled, authorities have said. Europol said 78 people were arrested in Spain and Algeria in a bust of the network, that is also linked to other criminal activities including "violent robberies, extortion, illegal detentions, and money laundering". The group moved synthetic drugs from Spain and Portugal to Algeria, then used the return journey to smuggle migrants and weapons to the Spanish mainland and island of Ibiza on "ghost speedboats". Some of the items seized included 18 high-speed vessels valued at €5m (£4.2m), guns, more than €25,000 (£21,400) in cash and 15,000 MDMA pills. The sting, led by Spanish police, involved searches in 17 locations in Spain, including Alicante, Almería, Cartagena and Murcia. Europol said the group had "evolved from drug trafficking into a duel-flow criminal enterprise designed to maximise profits" with outbound routes from Spain and Portugal to Algeria. "The smuggling focused on synthetic drugs (such as MDMA), firearms, and explosives. Along routine routes from Algeria to Spain, the group smuggled migrants, charging up to €12,000 (£10,200) per person," Europol's statement said. "In just one trip, over 50 migrants could be smuggled. All in all, profits from migrant smuggling alone are estimated to be more than €24m (£20m)." The network also provided services to other organised crime groups, "facilitating the movement of illicit goods and people across the Western Mediterranean". "Investigators believe the network coordinated multiple trafficking flows. Synthetic drugs, and sometimes people, were moved from France and Spain to Algeria, while cannabis resin, weapons, and migrants were transported from Algeria to Spain." Often, the group used a fleet of high-powered speedboats to conduct rapid maritime operations. This included "ghost speedboats" which are designed to avoid registration and detection, which are prohibited in Spain. "The group used these boats to organise transfers in international waters near the Spanish coastline," Europol said. "Once the cargo or migrants were handed over at sea, other network members arranged onward transport by land. "Migrants were often carried in overcrowded boats without lighting or life jackets, frequently under extreme weather conditions. "Investigators believe suspects perpetrated sexual assaults, physical abuse, and placed migrants in inhuman conditions in makeshift housing." The suspects were primarily of Algerian origin and had connections to criminal groups in France, Belgium, Portugal, Italy and Poland. Other objects seized in the police sting included satellite phones, GPS devices, encrypted communication tools and satellite dishes. The announcement comes a week after roughly 78,000 migrants fled into the Spanish North African territory of Ceuta that was blamed on online rumours about an open border. Most of the migrants returned to Morocco but between 3,000 and 5,000 remain in the territory, the exclave's leader Juan Jesús Vivas said. Related topics - Published7 days ago - Published29 July

item.title: Hunter Biden tells BBC his pardon was 'not good' for US or his father's legacy
item.description:

========================================
Hunter Biden tells BBC his pardon was 'not good' for US or his father's legacy - Published Hunter Biden has told the BBC he was "the most privileged person there is" after receiving a presidential pardon from his father, former US President Joe Biden, acknowledging that it was not a good choice for America or his father's legacy. In a wide-ranging interview with BBC Newsnight, Hunter Biden defended the controversial pardon, revealed his father's "painful" cancer has spread, ruled out seeking elected office and spoke about helping others recover from addiction. Asked about the 2024 pardon, he said he understood the criticism but noted: "What would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me." "It's something that is easily criticised and for good reason," he added. "It's not fair… All I know is that I'm grateful that he did it for me," he said, acknowledging the pardon was "not good" for the American people, the constitution - or his father's legacy. He argued to the BBC that his father ultimately acted out of concern that he would become a target under Donald Trump's incoming administration. "I was the only one in the world that could have gotten what I got from the only person in the world who could give it, my father." Hunter Biden also insisted he and his father had never discussed the possibility of a pardon before it was granted. "There is no way that you can have those kinds of discussions that would not become public," he said. President Biden granted his son a full and unconditional pardon in December 2024, despite repeatedly saying beforehand that he would not use the powers of the presidency to intervene in his son's legal cases. In announcing the decision, the former president said his son had been "selectively and unfairly prosecuted". The pardon covered his son's federal gun conviction, a tax case he'd pleaded guilty to and any federal offences committed between 2014 and 2024. Asked about the depths of his addiction, he described drinking almost a gallon of vodka a day while smoking crack cocaine almost every 15 minutes at its worst. "It was hell on earth," he said. "There's nothing glamorous about it." Reflecting on why he turned to drugs and alcohol, Hunter Biden rejected the suggestion that he felt untouchable because he was the son of a president. "I wasn't reaching for anything except oblivion," he said. He noted that his addiction was a way to escape feelings of anxiety and isolation. The drugs and alcohol initially felt like a solution before becoming "the thing that almost killed me", he noted. Hunter Biden got emotional at times in the interview, notably when discussing his father's health. "Cancer is really hard," he said, stopping to clear his throat. "It's really sad to watch." He revealed that the "cancer has spread, metastasised into his bones and further. It's very painful" and "very debilitating". "My dad is, to this day, the centre of our family," he said. "He's the best father, the best husband, the best grandfather." "The only thing that I say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more." Hunter Biden also reflected on the presidential debate in June 2024 that ultimately ended his father's re-election campaign. He said he had watched it from his home in California and immediately sensed something was wrong. "I was shocked," he said. "I knew something was wrong." Hunter Biden has previously argued that his father's poor debate performance reflected physical exhaustion after extensive travel. Following Joe Biden's cancer diagnosis, he has also questioned whether the illness may already have been affecting his father. He said his father remains politically engaged and determined to continue speaking publicly. When asked about rumours that he might enter politics - or even make a run for the presidency - Biden said he himself had "no interest in elected politics" and dismissed any suggestion that he would one day seek office. Instead, Biden said he wanted to devote his time to speaking about addiction and recovery, which he described as a cause capable of bridging America's political divides. "I believe that addiction and the hope of recovery are something that connect us all," he said. Asked what made him proudest of his father, Hunter Biden pointed not to his years in public office but to his resilience. "I'm most proud of his resilience," he said. "He's proven time and time again that when you get knocked down, you can get up. "He's the toughest man I know." item.title: Book hidden in fireplace returned to Australian library 150 years overdue
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39eprxln0go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Book hidden in fireplace returned to Australian library 150 years overdue - Published A book borrowed 150 years ago has finally been returned to an Australian library, with the culprit linked to the Houses of Parliament in London. Antiquities of Athens was borrowed from a local library in Kiama, a seaside town about 120km (75 miles) south of Sydney, some time in the mid-1870s. The book on classic Greek architecture was stored in a tea chest hidden behind a boarded-up fireplace for decades before it was recently discovered by a family member. Ross Simmons, 77, thinks his great-grandfather, John Simmons, might have borrowed the book to help with his career, having worked as an apprentice stonemason in Westminster in the mid-1800s before becoming an architect in Australia. Simmons, a self-confessed family history buff, said his great-grandfather studied in London between 1839 to 1844. "After his studies in London, he was apprenticed to other stonemasons to help in the construction of the Houses of Parliament," Simmons said. In 1857, aged 27, John Simmons emigrated from the UK to Australia, first living in the Sydney suburb of Newtown before relocating to Kiama after leading the construction of a sandstone church in the coastal town. "He had quite an interest in architecture, construction and building," Simmons said, adding that the overdue book "probably sat on a shelf at his house" and was used as a reference. The book somehow ended up in a tea chest - along with other family records - which was placed in a fireplace that was covered up. About 30 years ago, the tea chest was uncovered during renovations and the books - including the overdue one - were given to Simmons for safekeeping. But it wasn't until about a fortnight ago that he went through some of the books in greater detail. "I looked inside the front cover and, lo and behold, on the second page there was a Kiama Library stamp," Simmons said, with the library's borrowing conditions also detailed on the inside cover. For instance, library members could only borrow one book at a time, unless it could be proved that six people in the same household could read, in which case, three books could be lent out. Anyone intoxicated was barred from borrowing and members returning books past their due date would be fined three pence for every week it was late. Kiama Library staff worked out that the fine would be £97 - or in today's currency AU$28,000 ($20,000; £15,000), allowing for inflation. But luckily for the Simmons family, the fine has been waived. Kiama Council libraries manager Michelle Hudson said the unusual find had attracted a lot of attention. "People have travelled 40 minutes away to come and actually hold the book... it's a beautiful little book and it's got an amazing story to tell," she said. The cloth-bound volume has some water damage but otherwise, is in good condition, Hudson said. "It does have beautiful illustrations in it and some pages that fold out to show you they were using exact measurements of some of the monuments in Greece." She said in 1872, the council got a £200 grant to establish the town's library and and it had fewer than 1,000 books in its collection, with the overdue book marked as number 506. There's no way to know exactly who borrowed the book or when, Hudson said, as the library's borrowing records from that period have since been lost. However, the book is no longer available to borrow, having been added to the library's collection of special items, which can be viewed on request. "It won't be able to go out again... we don't want to wait another 150 years for it to come back," Hudson joked. As for the book's much-delayed return, Simmons said he believes his great-grandfather would be pleased with the final chapter of its journey. "I think he'd be happy to see the book returned and he'd probably have a bit of a laugh about it."

Kidnapped rare Serbian eagle freed into wild after rescue - Published A rare eastern imperial eagle has been rescued from animal traffickers and released back into the wild in Serbia after months in captivity. After leaving the nest last year, Feliks was caught in Syria by poachers who eventually demanded a ransom - which was refused. After protracted talks the bird was taken to a wildlife centre in Beirut, Lebanon, where he recuperated for more than half a year before his repatriation on a Serbian military plane. The protected species is critically endangered, but conservation work since 2017 has brought the population in Serbia from one pair up to 29 pairs this year, according to the Bird Protection and Study Society of Serbia (BPSSS). In July 2025, just as the young raptor first flew the nest, experts tracked him for conservation purposes as he flew towards the Middle East. "At that point, we started to worry because we could see that he was heading towards an extremely unsafe region," Uros Stojiljkovic of the BPSSS told the AFP news agency. When the bird's tracking signal was lost in October, initially it was thought the tracker was faulty. But it soon became clear Feliks had been abducted and eventually was put up for sale by poachers. Weeks passed before a partner organisation in Lebanon contacted the Serbian conservationist and said Feliks' unnamed captors had demanded a ransom. "We categorically refused. By doing so, you are effectively supporting that smuggling chain," Stojiljkovic told AFP. Lengthy negotiations secured the bird's release, but not before refugees carried Feliks in a potato sack over the Nahr al-Kabir river on the northern border between Syria and Lebanon, the Associated Press reported. In June this year, Serbian peacekeepers returning from Lebanon escorted the bird to Palic Zoo. Feliks arrived at the zoo's shelter "exhausted, after a long and demanding transport by military plane", zoo director Sonja Mandić said in a statement, and his health was monitored daily. After more than a month of careful recovery, Feliks was released into the wild on Thursday. "We wish Feliks to get stronger as soon as possible, survive all the adversities, conquer his territory and leave descendants," said Milan Ružić, executive director of the BPSSS. - Published6 August 2025 - Published29 March - Published10 July 2024

item.title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9q94lxqrzzo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope - Published "Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat. Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement. Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater. Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland – in the south-western corner of Australia – is one of the few places they remain. As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival. Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency. This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change. Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion. Australia has long been celebrated as a nature haven, home to some of the world's most unique plant and animal species. More than 80% cannot be found anywhere else. But it has arguably become the extinction capital of the world, losing roughly four species every decade - and the decline is only worsening. Dedicated volunteers and under-funded conservationists have been slowing the army of increasing threats, but experts fear that without urgent action and political courage, the biodiversity Australia says it loves is headed for a bloodbath. "It's not even a case of imagining it, it's happening in front of our own eyes," Professor Euan Ritchie tells the BBC. The many threats driving extinction If spotting a rare creature in the wild wasn't challenging enough, the numbat is a squirrel-sized camouflage connoisseur, explains Dr Tony Friend, the godfather of conservation in the state of Western Australia. "They just slept in today," jokes Rob McLean, president of the Numbat Taskforce, a volunteer group which makes a lot of Tony's thinly-resourced work possible. For two weeks each spring, as the young start venturing from their burrows, this team drives a daily circuit and records every numbat spotted. They log GPS coordinates, measure the distance to the road, and use a complicated equation to estimate the density of the animals in these woods and, from that, broader population health. One person sits in concentrated silence at each window, another perched in the back of the pick-up truck, ducking for the occasional limb branching from trees which rise around us. Through the trunks, we get the occasional glimpse of the razed farmland which tightly fences this pocket of protected woodland. On the side of one trail is a machine which detects and sprays feral cats and foxes with poison, another reminder of the perils numbats face. "This year's been a bit of a feast," Rob admits. For hours on end, we cruise around, seeing parrots, wallabies, a goanna and a couple of echidnas - but no numbats. Tony arrived at Dryandra back in the 80s to find a numbat population fewer than 50. Many of the culprits then were the same as those still driving extinctions across the nation today. Swathes of critical habitat are being cleared for development or industries like farming, mining and timber. Leaving a trail of destruction in their wake are introduced pests: fire ants, cane toads, rabbits, foxes, feral cats. Invasive weeds like lantana are choking the Australian bush, chlamydia has sent koalas to the edge of existence across much of the country, while the skin-eating chytrid fungus has caused seven frog extinctions here and counting. The changing climate is creating unliveable conditions for some species, like native flying foxes which are dropping out of trees in their thousands due to extreme temperatures. For others it is eliminating their food or their homes. Climate change is also driving natural disasters which fry and drown both plants and animals with now frightening regularity. The infamous Black Summer bushfires of 2019-20, for example, killed an estimated three billion animals. The successive years of record-breaking flooding which followed were so widespread it's impossible to estimate the impact on wildlife. Many species once abundant across the continent are now isolated to increasingly small and disjointed patches, each impact compounding and leaving them more vulnerable to the next. There are small, yet determined, efforts to slow the momentum of decline. As a young numbat scoffs his breakfast – custard with "termite sprinkles" – at Perth Zoo, a keeper explains how this stud's upcoming release at Dryandra will help boost genetic diversity. "When you get that feedback: your babies have got babies, it's very satisfying," Vicki Power says. Breeding programmes like this have also made setting up additional populations of an array of threatened species possible. But many cannot survive in the true wild, where large-scale predator control remains an endless battle, and are instead sent to fenced nature reserves, themselves high-maintenance undertakings facing problems like in-breeding and overpopulation. Habitat protection or restoration projects have been ramping up, but they are not keeping pace with destruction, particularly in the most critical areas. Scientists are also trying to fight disease, though that's an expensive and laborious endeavour, which for most species buys only a little more time. Others are preserving genetic material in case we ever work out how to resurrect species from the dead. A hundred species lost - and counting Scientists agree that we're living though the world's sixth mass extinction event, the first caused by humans. But Australia is at the front of this trend. It leads the world in mammal extinctions, and medals when it comes to the loss of other species classes too. "Despite Australia being one of the wealthiest countries per capita in the world and having more than its fair share of world-leading scientists… we have a truly awful record of conserving species," Ritchie says. "And things aren't getting better." The Australian government's official extinctions list sits at 67, but researchers are confident at least 100 plant and animal species have been lost forever. They suspect the true figure is far higher. The country is still discovering species which have already been wiped out. Though the rate of extinction in Australia has stayed stable, at around four per decade, the number of threatened species is still climbing quickly, and the deterioration of many is only gathering speed. This trajectory has some scary flow-on effects, experts warn. Australia's biodiversity "underpins everything", ecologist Jack Pascoe says. Think food production, tourism, construction – much of the economy. Potential scientific breakthroughs could be stymied: in medicine, agriculture and even climate change adaptation. And for First Nations Australians, the decline also threatens their culture. "We think of ourselves as custodians of all life on Earth… so there's a much more personal and social feeling of loss that comes when these things are not doing well or we lose them forever," Pascoe, a man from the Yuin Aboriginal nation, says. Decades of failures Though environment protection is a state responsibility, the federal government oversees matters of national importance. Labor took office in 2022, promising no new extinctions under its watch, and it has sought to make nature protection a defining feature of its second term. "It's well understood that nature is facing many challenges in the world today, both here in Australia, and overseas… we are losing biodiversity at an alarming rate," Environment Minister Murray Watt told the BBC in a statement. His party has significantly increased Australia's emissions reduction efforts and massively boosted renewable energy projects. There is some praise for their work on drawing critically endangered mammals back from the brink. And the passage of revamped environment laws last year was heralded as the most significant reform in a generation. The country also has an ambitious goal to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. But there's limited optimism that this will be a real turning point. The new laws are only the scaffolding of change. The substance of it is still being worked out – in the form of National Environmental Standards (NES) and a federal watchdog to enforce them. And many in the sector say the problem is not so much the regulatory tools available, but rather the political will to use them. Successive governments have failed to adequately protect the environment over the past 30 years, Australia's longest serving environment minister tells the BBC. That includes his own administration. "We should have done more too," says Robert Hill, who lead the last major reforms in 1999 under John Howard's conservative coalition. Many of the challenges of his era still haunt leaders today. The nation's wealth has largely been built off the back of its natural resources – often at the expense of the environment. Those riches still underpin the economy and help fund government spending on essentials like healthcare and housing. Then there's the added pressure applied by industry and the competing interests of states - whose stake in regulatory controls blurs the lines of accountability and increases bureaucratic hurdles. These battles leave even the toughest environmental advocates within governments bruised. For example, the Albanese government last year rushed through laws protecting salmon farming after lobbying by Tasmanian state officials, silencing opposition from within and ignoring advice from its own department concerning the impact of the A$1.4bn (£733m; $989m) industry on the survival of the Maugean Skate, an endangered ray. "The axe falls on the environmental outcome if there's the alternative of an economic one," Hill says. "Even if [the federal government] does want to act, it's still got to have the political strength to turn its aspirations into reality." There is also a belief that greater regulation alone will achieve little. Too much conservation work currently relies on philanthropists' cash and devoted volunteers, those in the sector say, and much more languishes on the to-do list due to a lack of money. The federal government directly spends about A$700m on nature protection, a fraction of the A$33bn – or 1% of GDP – conservationists say it should be. That is an eyebrow-raising figure, people like Paul Elton concede, but one they argue is reasonable. According to his research – which the government disputes – more than A$26bn is still being spent on subsidies for things like mining, intensive agriculture or fuel despite Australia signing global pledges to wind them back. "For every dollar the government is spending on positive biodiversity conservation action, there's A$26 being spent on subsidies that are causing harm to nature," he tells the BBC. "That's a pretty stark imbalance." Minister Watt didn't directly respond to questions about conservationists' demands, but said: "We remain committed to long-term environmental recovery, in partnership with state and local governments, community and environmental groups." Though public sentiment is shifting, there's scepticism the government will prioritise the environment amid competing demands and compounding crises until voters force them to do so. "The community will say to you, we should spend a lot of money on the environment. And then if you say, 'Well, what are you prepared to sacrifice to ensure that funding base?', then they're no longer interested," Hill says. In the face of so many challenges and what they see as little progress, advocates admit it's hard to hang on to hope. "We know what the problems are. We know how to address them. We know when we spend money on the environment, it pays back many times over," Ritchie, a mammal ecologist, says. "It's like being a doctor and seeing all these sick people in the community and you know how to fix them, but no one will let you do that." Small wins, like the future of the numbat, keep them fighting. There are now around 3,000 nationwide, and in Dryandra numbers have increased ten-fold. The animal has recently been taken off the international endangered species list and is now classified as near-threatened. It takes five hours, but finally synchronised cries of excitement come from the driver's seat and the back of the pick-up truck. The cause of the commotion stands frozen and alert at the end of a hollowing log. "It's not a competition," Rob says. Chuckling, he points at his rival spotter: "But I beat him by a second." The dam has broken. Over the next little while we see eight numbats, including two pairs of babies, blinking at us in the dusky light. This year's full count, Tony later tells me, is one of the best yet. "But I remind people they're not out of the woods yet," Tony says. The relief at the numbat's revival is tempered by worry this will make it harder to access the funding and support needed to cement those gains. The woylie, or brush-tailed bettong, is a cautionary tale. It recovered slightly and was taken off the threatened list only to be added again a decade later, in a worse state. "We can't walk away," Tony says, "and say 'no, they're fine,' you know?" "It's got to be accepted that continued work is needed to keep that animal on the planet."
